title: Acasta Gneiss: oldest intact rocks
summary: Granitic crust crystallizes in what is now Canada's Northwest Territories, forming the oldest known intact rocks on Earth.
description: The Acasta Gneiss, exposed along the Acasta River about 300 km north of Yellowknife, contains tonalitic and granitic gneisses whose zircons, dated by Samuel Bowring and colleagues, give uranium–lead crystallization ages of about 4.03 billion years, and some grains contain inherited cores about 4.2 billion years old. They are the oldest dated intact rocks known; older Hadean material survives only as individual zircon grains, such as those from the Jack Hills of Western Australia. Their chemistry suggests they formed by the remelting of even older, basaltic crust. The International Commission on Stratigraphy places the start of the Archean at 4,031 million years ago, matching the age of these rocks. Claims that parts of Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt are older remain disputed.

title: Fringe: life seeded on Earth from Mars
summary: A speculative hypothesis proposes that life began on early Mars and reached Earth inside rocks blasted off the planet by impacts.
description: Some researchers have suggested that life originated on Mars around 4 billion years ago and was carried to Earth inside meteorites, a variant of panspermia often called lithopanspermia. Proponents argue that early Mars may have offered drier land surfaces and minerals, such as borates and oxidized molybdenum, thought to favour prebiotic chemistry, and note that rocks still travel from Mars to Earth today. The idea drew wide attention in 1996, when NASA scientists reported possible microfossils in the Martian meteorite ALH84001, found in the Allan Hills of Antarctica. It remains an untested speculation rather than an established account of life's origin.
mainstreamView: Rock transfer from Mars is real: hundreds of Martian meteorites are known, and some, like ALH84001, were never heated enough to sterilize their interiors. But no life, past or present, has been found on Mars, and the ALH84001 'microfossils' are now widely attributed to non-biological processes. The prebiotic-chemistry arguments for Mars are contested and early Earth appears to have offered comparable conditions, so most origin-of-life researchers see no evidence requiring a Martian origin; the idea is treated as a speculative possibility, not a supported theory.

title: Fringe: life delivered by comets
summary: Fred Hoyle and Chandra Wickramasinghe argued that living cells arrived on Earth aboard comets and are still arriving from space today.
description: From the 1970s, astronomers Fred Hoyle and Chandra Wickramasinghe argued that life did not originate on Earth but was delivered as bacteria and viruses frozen in comets, beginning with the heavy bombardment of the early Archean. In their model, often called cometary panspermia or cosmic ancestry, microbes are widespread in interstellar dust and new arrivals continue to this day, even causing epidemics such as influenza. Wickramasinghe and colleagues later claimed to find fossil diatoms in stones that fell near Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka, in 2012. The hypothesis is notable because Hoyle was a leading astrophysicist, but it is not accepted by biologists or astronomers.
mainstreamView: Comets and meteorites do carry organic molecules, including the amino acid glycine detected at comet 67P and in samples returned from comet Wild 2, so space may have delivered some raw ingredients for life. However, no living or fossil cells have been verified in any comet or meteorite. The interstellar infrared spectra that Hoyle and Wickramasinghe read as bacterial are explained by non-biological organic and silicate grains, and the Polonnaruwa 'diatoms' are regarded as terrestrial contamination, with doubts that the stones were meteorites at all. Pathogens are closely adapted to their hosts and their genomes show they evolved on Earth, so claims of epidemics from space are rejected.

title: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)
summary: The last common ancestor of all living things, a population of simple cells, gives rise to the bacterial and archaeal lineages.
description: Every known organism shares the same genetic code, core metabolic machinery and hundreds of genes, implying descent from a last universal common ancestor, or LUCA. Reconstructions based on genes shared by bacteria and archaea suggest LUCA was a prokaryote-like cell, probably anaerobic, that used hydrogen and carbon dioxide and may have lived in or near hydrothermal settings. Its age is uncertain: molecular-clock studies range from about 3.5 billion years to more than 4.2 billion years, and a 2024 study placed it near 4.2 billion years ago, in the Hadean. LUCA was not the first life; it was the last ancestor of the lineages that survive, and it probably lived alongside other organisms whose lineages died out.
mainstreamView: That all life descends from a common ancestor is firmly established by shared genetics and biochemistry. What is debated is when LUCA lived, whether it inhabited hot hydrothermal settings or more moderate environments, and how complex it was. The date shown here is a representative midpoint of published estimates, not a measured age.

title: Fringe: directed panspermia
summary: Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel speculated that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization deliberately seeded the young Earth with microbes.
description: In a 1973 paper in the journal Icarus, Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel proposed that life on Earth might descend from microorganisms deliberately sent by an extraterrestrial civilization, arriving on the young Earth around the time life first appears in the rock record. They offered it as a provocative alternative to an origin on Earth, citing the universality of the genetic code and the biological importance of the rare element molybdenum as puzzles it might explain. Crick expanded on the idea in his 1981 book Life Itself. Variants of the notion have since appeared in science fiction and in some intelligent-design arguments.
mainstreamView: Crick and Orgel themselves presented directed panspermia as a speculation, and no evidence has emerged to support it. It does not explain how life began, only moves the problem to another world, and it cannot currently be tested. The universal genetic code is explained by all life descending from a single common ancestor, and molybdenum's role in enzymes is explained by its distinctive chemistry. Origin-of-life research instead focuses on plausible chemical pathways on the early Earth.

title: Isua Greenstone Belt: ancient sea floor in Greenland
summary: Lavas and sediments laid down on an ancient sea floor in southwest Greenland survive as some of the oldest well-preserved volcanic and sedimentary rocks.
description: The Isua Greenstone Belt, about 150 km northeast of Nuuk, preserves volcanic and sedimentary rocks formed roughly 3.8–3.7 billion years ago. Pillow lavas, which form only when lava erupts under water, and banded iron formations show that oceans existed by this time. Graphite in metamorphosed sediments is enriched in the light carbon-12 isotope, a pattern many researchers interpret as one of the earliest chemical traces of life, though intense metamorphism makes this hard to prove. Some geologists also read Isua's structures as evidence of early subduction-like tectonics, an interpretation that remains contested.

title: Sulfur isotopes reveal an oxygen-free atmosphere
summary: Unusual sulfur isotope ratios, which survive only when the air lacks oxygen, show that the Archean atmosphere held almost no free oxygen.
description: Most chemical and biological processes separate the isotopes of sulfur in proportion to their mass, but in 2000 James Farquhar, Huiming Bao and Mark Thiemens showed that sulfur minerals in Archean rocks carry an anomalous, mass-independent fractionation, known as MIF-S. Experiments and models link this signal to the breakdown of volcanic sulfur dioxide by ultraviolet sunlight in an atmosphere with no ozone layer. It can be preserved in sediments only if oxygen was below roughly one hundred-thousandth of today's level, because otherwise the different sulfur products would be oxidized and mixed back together. MIF-S is found in sedimentary rocks as old as about 3.8 billion years, is weaker between about 3.2 and 2.7 billion years ago, and disappears during the Great Oxidation Event, making its loss one of the clearest markers of that transition. A minority of researchers argues that some of the signal could form through non-atmospheric reactions, but the atmospheric explanation is widely accepted.

title: Nuvvuagittuq: oldest fossils, or chemical mimics?
summary: Iron-oxide tubes in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt were reported in 2017 as fossils of vent microbes at least 3.77 billion years old; the claim is contested.
description: The Nuvvuagittuq Greenstone Belt, on the eastern shore of Hudson Bay in northern Quebec, contains metamorphosed sea-floor volcanic rocks and iron-rich jaspers at least 3.75–3.78 billion years old, although a disputed neodymium-isotope age of 4.28 billion years has also been proposed. In 2017 Matthew Dodd and colleagues described microscopic tubes and filaments of haematite in the jaspers, together with graphite, carbonate and apatite, and interpreted them as fossils of iron-oxidizing microbes that lived around sea-floor hydrothermal vents at least 3.77 billion years ago. If accepted, they would be older than the 3.48-billion-year-old Pilbara stromatolites, the oldest widely accepted evidence of life.
mainstreamView: A minimum age of about 3.75–3.78 billion years for the host rocks is widely accepted, while the older 4.28-billion-year age is disputed. The putative microfossils are contested: similar tubes and filaments of iron oxide can grow through purely chemical reactions, as in laboratory 'chemical gardens', and the rocks have been strongly heated and deformed. Later work by members of the original team describing larger branching structures has not settled the debate.

title: Disputed 3.7-billion-year-old stromatolites
summary: Centimetre-high cones in Greenland's Isua belt were announced in 2016 as the oldest stromatolites, built by microbial mats 3.7 billion years ago.
description: In 2016 a team led by Allen Nutman reported small conical and domed layered structures, 1–4 cm tall, in dolomite of the Isua Greenstone Belt that had recently been exposed by melting snow. They interpreted them as stromatolites, mounds built by layered microbial communities in shallow seawater, which would push the fossil record of life back by more than 200 million years. A 2018 re-examination led by Abigail Allwood argued that the shapes are the product of tectonic deformation of layered rock and that their internal structure and chemistry are not biological.
mainstreamView: The claim remains contested. Supporters point to the structures' shapes and to trace-element patterns resembling seawater sediments, while critics showed that in three dimensions the 'cones' are elongated ridges consistent with folding. Many researchers regard the 3.48-billion-year-old stromatolites of the Pilbara as the oldest widely accepted examples.

title: Oldest record of Earth's magnetic field
summary: Iron-rich rocks in Greenland's Isua belt preserve a magnetic field comparable in strength to today's, the oldest well-supported record of Earth's geodynamo.
description: Earth's magnetic field is generated by the churning of liquid iron in the outer core, a process called the geodynamo, and it helps shield the atmosphere and surface from the solar wind and cosmic radiation. Iron minerals can lock in the direction and strength of the field when they form or are heated, but most Archean rocks have been reheated too often to keep a reliable record. In 2024 a team led by Claire Nichols reported that banded iron formations of the Isua Supracrustal Belt retain a magnetization acquired about 3.7 billion years ago, recording a field of at least 15 microteslas, comparable to the roughly 30 microteslas of today's field. This extends earlier evidence from 3.45-billion-year-old rocks of South Africa's Barberton belt, which John Tarduno and colleagues reported in 2010 as recording a field about half to 70% as strong as today's. Claims that 4.2-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircons record an even older field remain disputed.

title: Vaalbara: the first supercraton?
summary: South Africa's Kaapvaal and Australia's Pilbara cratons may once have been joined as Vaalbara, a candidate for Earth's earliest supercontinent.
description: The Kaapvaal Craton of southern Africa, whose oldest nucleus in Eswatini is about 3.6 billion years old, and the Pilbara Craton of Western Australia contain strikingly similar sequences of Archean volcanic and sedimentary rocks. Both also preserve matching layers of impact spherules, the debris of giant asteroid strikes. These parallels led geologists to propose that the two cratons formed a single landmass, named Vaalbara from KaapVAAL and PilBARA, from roughly 3.6 to 2.7 billion years ago. If so, it would be one of the earliest known continental blocks larger than a single craton.
mainstreamView: Paleomagnetic data from about 2.78 billion years ago have been interpreted as supporting a connection, and the shared spherule beds suggest the cratons were at least near each other. But other paleomagnetic reconstructions place them far apart by 2.7 billion years ago, and similar rock sequences can form on separate cratons, so whether Vaalbara existed, and for how long, remains unresolved.

title: Siurua gneiss: oldest rock in the Fennoscandian Shield
summary: Trondhjemite magma crystallizes in what is now northern Finland, forming the oldest rock known in the Fennoscandian Shield and the European Union.
description: The Siurua trondhjemite gneiss, in the Pudasjärvi area of northern Finland, has yielded zircon uranium–lead ages of about 3.5 billion years, making it the oldest rock identified in the Fennoscandian Shield and the European Union; older Eoarchean rocks, up to about 3.75 billion years old, occur in the Podolian Domain of the Ukrainian Shield. It lies within the Karelian Province, a block of Archean crust that forms the ancient core of Fennoscandia. Like other Archean trondhjemites it belongs to the tonalite–trondhjemite–granodiorite (TTG) family, the characteristic rocks of Earth's earliest continental crust.

title: Komatiite lavas of the Barberton belt
summary: Extremely hot, magnesium-rich lavas erupt in the Barberton region of South Africa, revealing a mantle far hotter than today's.
description: Komatiites are ultramafic lavas named after the Komati River in South Africa's Barberton Greenstone Belt, where they were first recognized in the 1960s in the Komati Formation, dated to about 3.48 billion years ago. Their high magnesium content implies eruption temperatures of roughly 1,600 °C, several hundred degrees hotter than modern basalts, and many show spinifex texture, long bladed olivine crystals formed by rapid cooling. Komatiites are common in Archean greenstone belts worldwide but almost absent from younger rocks, making them key evidence that Earth's mantle was considerably hotter in the Archean. A minority view holds that dissolved water lowered their melting temperature, which would reduce the inferred mantle temperatures. The Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018 for their exceptionally preserved Archean rocks.

title: Dresser Formation: oldest accepted stromatolites
summary: Microbial mats build layered stromatolites around hot springs and shallow pools in Western Australia, the oldest widely accepted evidence of life.
description: The Dresser Formation in the North Pole Dome of the Pilbara Craton contains wrinkly, domed and conical stromatolites about 3.48 billion years old, interlayered with chert and barite. Most researchers accept them as the oldest convincing fossils, and a 2019 study found organic matter preserved within pyritized stromatolites, strengthening the case that microbes built them. Geyserite and other hot-spring deposits described in 2017 suggest some of these microbial communities lived on land around volcanic hot springs, a possible clue to where early life flourished. Sulfur and carbon isotopes in the formation have also been read as signs of microbial sulfate reduction and methane production, though those interpretations are more debated.

title: Apex Chert microfossil controversy
summary: Tiny carbon filaments in the Apex Chert near Marble Bar, Australia, were claimed as Earth's oldest microfossils, sparking a decades-long debate.
description: In 1993 J. William Schopf described chains of cell-like carbonaceous filaments in the 3.465-billion-year-old Apex Chert of the Pilbara and interpreted them as microfossils resembling cyanobacteria, then the oldest known. In 2002 Martin Brasier and colleagues argued that the chert formed in a hydrothermal vein and that the filaments were non-biological carbon artefacts, and later studies suggested some of the structures are mineral growths. In 2018 Schopf's team reported carbon-isotope differences among the filament types that they read as evidence of distinct microbial metabolisms.
mainstreamView: Opinion remains divided. Life almost certainly existed by this time, given stromatolites in nearby formations, but many specialists consider the Apex filaments pseudofossils formed by non-biological processes in a hydrothermal setting. The case is now often cited as a cautionary example in the search for early life on Earth and Mars.

title: Strelley Pool stromatolite reef
summary: A shallow carbonate platform in Western Australia hosts a diverse 'reef' of stromatolites, strong evidence that microbial life was widespread.
description: The Strelley Pool Formation of the Pilbara contains stromatolites in at least seven distinct shapes, traced across a carbonate platform roughly 10 km long, as documented by Abigail Allwood and colleagues in 2006. Their variety, and the way their forms change with ancient water depth and setting, are hard to explain without biology, so they are widely accepted as built by microbial communities. In 2011 a team reported microfossils in sandstone at the base of the formation, with associated pyrite suggesting the cells metabolized sulfur. Together these finds indicate that by 3.4 billion years ago microbial ecosystems occupied a range of shallow-marine environments.

title: Singhbhum Craton rises above the sea
summary: Thickened granitic crust in eastern India lifts above sea level, one of the earliest large-scale emergences of continental land.
description: A 2021 study of the Singhbhum Craton in Jharkhand and Odisha found ancient river and coastal sandstones resting on granitic crust and argued that the whole craton became dry land about 3.3–3.2 billion years ago. The authors proposed that voluminous granitic magmatism thickened the crust and made it buoyant enough to rise above the sea, without requiring plate tectonics. Emergent land matters for the whole Earth system, because weathering of exposed rock delivers nutrients such as phosphorus to the oceans and draws down atmospheric carbon dioxide.
mainstreamView: When substantial continents first emerged is debated. Smaller patches of land existed earlier, as shown by 3.48-billion-year-old hot-spring deposits in the Pilbara, while some studies argue that large-scale emergence came only near the end of the Archean, around 2.5 billion years ago. The Singhbhum work is a well-documented case for early emergence, but it concerns a single craton and its significance for global land area is uncertain.

title: S2 giant impact
summary: An asteroid perhaps 37–58 km across strikes Earth, leaving a spherule bed in South Africa's Barberton belt and churning the oceans.
description: The Barberton Greenstone Belt preserves at least eight layers of impact spherules, droplets of melted rock thrown around the globe by large asteroid strikes between about 3.47 and 3.23 billion years ago. The best studied, the S2 bed, records an impactor estimated at 37–58 km across, with 50–200 times the mass of the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs. Its crater has long since been destroyed, but the deposits record a tsunami that tore up the sea floor, partial boiling of the surface ocean and a dust cloud that darkened the sky. A 2024 study found that microbial life recovered quickly and may even have benefited from the pulse of iron and phosphorus that the impact stirred up.

title: Tidal layers record a closer Moon
summary: Tide-laid sandstones in South Africa's Moodies Group suggest the Moon orbited about 70% as far away and days lasted roughly 13 hours.
description: Tidal friction gradually transfers Earth's rotational momentum to the Moon's orbit, so over billions of years Earth's spin has slowed and the Moon has receded; today it moves away by about 3.8 cm per year. Sandstone–mudstone layers in the 3.22-billion-year-old Moodies Group of the Barberton Greenstone Belt show cycles of about 15 layers that researchers interpret as spring–neap tidal bundles. A 2023 analysis used this periodicity to estimate that the Moon was about 70% of its present distance and that a day lasted around 13 hours. Because the result depends on assumptions about how the layers were deposited, such estimates carry large uncertainties.

title: Plate tectonics begins (debated)
dateLabel: c. 3.2 billion years ago (estimates range widely)
summary: Earth's outer shell may have broken into moving, subducting plates around 3.2–3.0 billion years ago, though the timing is hotly debated.
description: Today Earth's lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that spread apart at mid-ocean ridges and sink back into the mantle at subduction zones, recycling crust and regulating long-term climate. In the hotter early Archean many geologists think the crust behaved differently, as a 'stagnant' or 'squishy' lid dominated by vertical, drip-like tectonics, which may explain the dome-and-keel patterns of the older Pilbara crust. Several lines of evidence point to a shift around 3.2–3.0 billion years ago: changes in the chemistry of new continental crust recorded by zircons, eclogite-type inclusions in diamonds that appear only after about 3 billion years ago, and paleomagnetic data suggesting the Pilbara was drifting about 3.2 billion years ago. Published estimates nonetheless range from the Hadean to as late as about 0.8 billion years ago.
mainstreamView: Most geologists accept that some form of plate tectonics was operating by the late Archean, about 2.5 billion years ago, and many favour a gradual or episodic onset around 3.2–3.0 billion years ago. A minority argues for subduction already in the Hadean, while others maintain that modern-style plate tectonics, with the cold, deep subduction recorded by blueschists and ultra-high-pressure rocks, began only in the Neoproterozoic.

title: Earliest evidence of nitrogen fixation
summary: Nitrogen isotopes in 3.2-billion-year-old sediments suggest microbes were already turning inert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable nutrient.
description: All organisms need nitrogen to build proteins and nucleic acids, but the nitrogen gas that makes up most of the atmosphere is chemically inert, and only some microbes can convert it into ammonia using the enzyme nitrogenase. Without biological fixation, life would have depended on small supplies of fixed nitrogen made by lightning and volcanic processes, limiting the size of the early biosphere. In 2015 Eva Stüeken, Roger Buick and colleagues reported that nitrogen isotope ratios in marine and river sediments 3.2 to 2.75 billion years old fall in a narrow range best explained by fixation with the molybdenum-based form of nitrogenase, the most common type today. The result implies that biological nitrogen fixation is at least 3.2 billion years old, and that molybdenum was less scarce in the oxygen-poor oceans than some researchers had assumed.

title: Ur: a hypothesized early continent
summary: Cratons now in India, southern Africa, Western Australia and Antarctica may have been joined as Ur, proposed as one of Earth's first continents.
description: In the 1990s geologist John J. W. Rogers proposed that several Archean cratons, now found in India (including the Dharwar and Singhbhum cratons), southern Africa, Western Australia and East Antarctica, assembled about 3.1 billion years ago into a continent he named Ur in 1993 and reconstructed in detail in 1996. Though probably smaller than modern Australia, it would have been one of the first sizeable landmasses. Rogers suggested that Ur persisted as a coherent block for a very long time and was later incorporated into larger supercontinents.
mainstreamView: Ur is a hypothesis based largely on similarities in rock ages and types rather than on firm paleomagnetic data. Reliable paleomagnetic reconstructions this old are scarce, and many geologists doubt that these cratons were joined so early or stayed together; Ur is best regarded as a speculative reconstruction.

title: Lewisian gneiss forms in Scotland
summary: Granitic and mafic magmas crystallize deep in the crust, forming the rocks that become Scotland's Lewisian gneiss, Britain's oldest.
description: The Lewisian complex of northwest Scotland and the Outer Hebrides consists of banded gneisses whose oldest components, the Scourie complex around Scourie in Sutherland, crystallized from granitic and mafic magmas about 3.0–2.7 billion years ago. The rocks were later deformed and metamorphosed deep in the crust during several events lasting into the Paleoproterozoic. Named after the Isle of Lewis, they are the oldest rocks in Britain and a fragment of ancient crust once continuous with Archean rocks now in Greenland and Labrador. Their relationship to younger rocks along the Moine Thrust made the region a classic site in the history of geology.

title: Fringe: Klerksdorp spheres as ancient artifacts
dateLabel: c. 3 billion years ago (age of the host rock)
summary: Grooved balls from a South African pyrophyllite mine have been promoted as 3-billion-year-old artifacts; geologists identify them as natural concretions.
description: Klerksdorp spheres are small spherical to disc-shaped objects, some with a groove around their middle, that miners have collected from pyrophyllite deposits, sold as 'wonderstone', near Ottosdal in South Africa's North West Province. The host rock, part of the Mesoarchean Dominion Group, formed from volcanic material and lake muds roughly 3 billion years ago. From the 1980s, books, magazines and websites presented the spheres as out-of-place artifacts made by intelligent beings, describing them as perfectly round, harder than steel and made of unknown alloys. Stories also claimed that one rotated by itself in a display case at the Klerksdorp Museum, after which the spheres are named.
mainstreamView: Geologists who have examined the spheres, including Bruce Cairncross and Paul Heinrich, identify them as natural concretions that grew within the volcanic sediments after deposition and were altered during later metamorphism. They consist of hematite, or of wollastonite with minor hematite and goethite, and some unweathered specimens still contain pyrite; none is a manufactured alloy, and they are neither perfectly round nor unusually hard. The grooves follow fine-grained layers in the host rock that slowed the concretions' growth, much like the ridges on Utah's Moqui marbles. The museum curator's remarks were misreported, and any movement in the display case has been attributed to vibrations from underground blasting at nearby gold mines.

title: Witwatersrand gold deposits accumulate
summary: Rivers spread gold-bearing gravels into a basin around present-day Johannesburg, building the richest gold field ever found.
description: Over some 260 million years, rivers and deltas carried sand and gravel into the Witwatersrand Basin on the Kaapvaal Craton, concentrating gold in conglomerate layers known as reefs. Since their discovery in 1886 these deposits have yielded more than 40,000 tonnes of gold, more than any other region on Earth, and led to the founding of Johannesburg. The conglomerates also contain rounded grains of pyrite and uraninite, minerals that would be oxidized and destroyed in streams under today's oxygen-rich atmosphere, making them key evidence that Archean air held little free oxygen. Most geologists regard the gold as river-concentrated placer gold later modified by hot fluids, though the roles of hydrothermal fluids and microbial mats remain debated.

title: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolves
summary: Ancestors of cyanobacteria evolve oxygen-releasing photosynthesis; local oxygen traces hint it existed by 2.95 billion years ago, but the timing is debated.
description: Oxygenic photosynthesis uses sunlight to split water, releasing oxygen as a by-product; it evolved in the ancestors of cyanobacteria and was later passed to algae and plants through endosymbiosis. At first its oxygen did not accumulate in the atmosphere, because it was consumed by dissolved iron, sulfur compounds and volcanic gases. Geochemical signals in South Africa's Pongola Supergroup about 2.95 billion years old, including manganese enrichments and chromium and molybdenum isotope patterns, have been interpreted as local 'oases' of free oxygen produced by these microbes. Lasting oxygen in the atmosphere arrived only with the Great Oxidation Event, beginning around 2.4 billion years ago.
mainstreamView: Nearly all researchers agree that oxygenic photosynthesis existed before the Great Oxidation Event, but its origin date is debated. Some argue for an origin before 3.5 billion years ago, while others interpret the early 'oxygen oases' as artefacts and place the innovation shortly before 2.4 billion years ago. Biomarker molecules once taken as evidence for cyanobacteria 2.7 billion years ago were later shown to be contamination, so the case rests mainly on indirect geochemistry and molecular clocks.

title: Pongola glaciation: oldest known ice age
summary: Glaciers leave boulder-strewn deposits in what is now South Africa, the earliest well-documented glaciation on Earth.
description: Diamictites in the Mozaan Group of the Pongola Supergroup, in northern KwaZulu-Natal and southern Mpumalanga, contain striated pebbles and dropstones showing deposition by glaciers and floating ice about 2.9 billion years ago. Glacial deposits of similar age also occur in the nearby Witwatersrand Supergroup. It is the oldest known glaciation, occurring when the young Sun was roughly 20% fainter than today and Earth's warmth depended on greenhouse gases. Its cause is uncertain, possibly a drop in atmospheric methane or carbon dioxide, and it is unknown whether it was a regional ice cap or a more widespread glaciation.

title: Fortescue and Ventersdorp flood basalts erupt
summary: Vast outpourings of lava flood the Pilbara and Kaapvaal cratons, building some of Earth's oldest well-preserved large igneous provinces.
description: Between about 2.78 and 2.71 billion years ago, kilometres-thick piles of basaltic and other volcanic rocks accumulated on the Pilbara Craton of Western Australia, in the Fortescue Group, and on the Kaapvaal Craton of southern Africa, in the Ventersdorp Supergroup. Erupted over wide areas as the continental crust was stretched and rifted, they are among the oldest well-preserved large igneous provinces. Many geologists link them to mantle plumes, or to a broader episode of plume activity around 2.7 billion years ago that coincided with a worldwide pulse of crust formation. The similar ages and sequences of the two provinces are also used to argue that the cratons were joined as Vaalbara. Their lavas and ash beds preserve clues to the Archean environment, including fossil raindrop imprints and lava bubbles used to estimate ancient air pressure.

title: Banded iron formations: Carajás
summary: Iron-rich layers settle on the sea floor in Amazonia, forming the Carajás deposit, now one of the world's largest sources of iron ore.
description: Banded iron formations are finely layered sedimentary rocks of alternating iron oxides and silica that precipitated from oceans rich in dissolved ferrous iron, which can build up only in seawater lacking oxygen. They first appear at Isua in Greenland about 3.8 billion years ago, peak between about 2.6 and 2.4 billion years ago, and largely disappear after about 1.85 billion years ago. The Carajás Formation in Pará, Brazil, deposited about 2.75 billion years ago, hosts the Carajás mine, one of the largest iron ore mines on Earth. How the iron was oxidized is debated: oxygen from early cyanobacteria, iron-oxidizing photosynthetic bacteria and ultraviolet light have all been proposed.

title: Kenorland supercontinent assembles
summary: A global pulse of continent building welds Archean cratons together, possibly forming Kenorland, a candidate early supercontinent.
description: Around 2.7 billion years ago Earth experienced one of the largest pulses of continental crust formation in its history, building extensive granite–greenstone terrains such as the Abitibi belt of Canada's Superior Craton. Collisions during the Kenoran orogeny, named after Kenora in Ontario, sutured many of these blocks together. Some geologists infer that much of the continental crust then merged into a supercontinent called Kenorland, including parts of what are now North America, Fennoscandia, Western Australia and southern Africa. Swarms of mafic dykes dated to about 2.48–2.45 billion years ago are often read as evidence that it rifted apart near the start of the Proterozoic.
mainstreamView: That a major crust-building and collisional episode occurred around 2.7 billion years ago is well established. Whether it produced a single supercontinent is debated: paleomagnetic data are sparse, and many researchers instead favour several separate 'supercratons', such as Superia, Sclavia and Vaalbara, that assembled and broke up at different times.

title: Fossil raindrops and lava bubbles gauge the air
summary: Fossil raindrop imprints in South Africa and gas bubbles in Australian lavas suggest the late Archean air was no denser than today's, perhaps much thinner.
description: How dense the early atmosphere was matters for explaining how Earth stayed warm under a fainter Sun, because a thicker atmosphere strengthens the effect of greenhouse gases. In 2012 Sanjoy Som, David Catling and colleagues compared fossil raindrop imprints in 2.7-billion-year-old volcanic ash of South Africa's Ventersdorp Supergroup with imprints made by water drops in modern ash, and concluded that air density was less than twice the modern value and probably close to or below it. In 2016 the same group measured gas bubbles at the tops and bottoms of lava flows that solidified at sea level about 2.74 billion years ago in Western Australia's Pilbara, and inferred a surface pressure of only about 0.23 bar, less than half of today's. If correct, the warmth of the late Archean must have depended on high concentrations of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane rather than on a dense nitrogen atmosphere.
mainstreamView: Both methods are new and rest on assumptions, such as the largest size ancient raindrops could reach and how bubbles were trapped in cooling lava, and other researchers have questioned how tightly they constrain the pressure. Nitrogen isotopes in fluid inclusions from 3.5-billion-year-old quartz in the Pilbara likewise suggest that nitrogen pressure was no higher than today's. Most researchers accept that the Archean atmosphere was not much denser than the modern one, but whether it was substantially thinner remains debated.

title: Methane greenhouse and organic haze
summary: Microbial methane warms Earth under a faint young Sun and at times may thicken into an orange organic haze like that of Saturn's moon Titan.
description: The young Sun shone 20–25% less brightly than today, yet geological evidence shows liquid water through most of the Archean, a puzzle known as the faint young Sun paradox. A likely part of the answer is a strong greenhouse effect from carbon dioxide and methane, the latter produced by methanogenic microbes in the oxygen-poor environment. Models show that when methane becomes abundant relative to carbon dioxide, sunlight converts it into a hydrocarbon haze, as on Titan. Sulfur and carbon isotope excursions in 2.65–2.5-billion-year-old rocks of South Africa's Ghaap Group have been interpreted as records of repeated haze episodes, which would have cooled the surface and screened out ultraviolet light.
mainstreamView: That methane contributed substantially to Archean warmth is widely accepted, although the relative roles of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrogen pressure and clouds in resolving the faint young Sun paradox are still debated. The haze episodes are inferred from indirect isotope signals that some researchers attribute to other processes, so their existence and frequency remain uncertain.

title: A 'whiff' of oxygen before the Great Oxidation
summary: Shales in Western Australia's Hamersley Basin record a brief rise in oxygen about 2.5 billion years ago, a prelude to the Great Oxidation Event.
description: In 2007 two studies of the Mount McRae Shale, sampled in a drill core from the Hamersley Basin, reported enrichments of molybdenum and rhenium and shifts in sulfur isotopes in rocks about 2.5 billion years old. Because these metals are released mainly by oxidative weathering of continental rocks, the authors interpreted the signals as a transient 'whiff' of oxygen in the atmosphere some 50–100 million years before the Great Oxidation Event. The finding suggested that oxygenic photosynthesis was already active and that oxygen rose in fits and starts.
mainstreamView: The interpretation was challenged in 2022 by a study arguing that the metal enrichments were introduced by later fluids long after deposition; other researchers have defended the original interpretation with additional data. Most scientists agree that oxygenic photosynthesis preceded the Great Oxidation Event, but whether the Mount McRae Shale records true atmospheric oxygen remains debated.
